title: Separating Long vs Short parameter search in Walk-Forward Optimizers — how do you handle directional asymmetry without overfitting?
author: Trader_for_earner
selftext:
Hey guys,

Looking for some perspective from anyone running portfolio-level walk-forward optimizers on crypto perpetuals or equities.

Lately we’ve been auditing our cross-sectional universe optimizer across a basket of \~15 altcoins. Up until now, when we run our in-sample grid search across our setups (mostly mean-reversion like VWAP deviations and momentum break-and-retests), the optimizer searched for a single shared "centroid" parameter set for both Longs and Shorts simultaneously (e.g. optimizing band stretch deviation, RSI cutoffs, and ATR stop/take multiples together).

The problem we ran into in live execution: During recent relief rallies and fast trend shifts, we got caught in a string of Short SL hits on mean-reversion setups. When we looked under the hood and decomposed the trades by side, the asymmetry was wild:

Longs were printing a 2.5–3.5 Profit Factor across coins like NEAR and DOT using relatively loose pullbacks.

Shorts on those exact same parameter settings were getting wrecked (PF < 0.8), repeatedly fading momentum too early in cascade environments.

Because the optimizer averaged both directions together in-sample, the strong Long trades were effectively "subsidizing" and masking a negative-expectancy Short setting. The compromised shared centroid ended up being sub-optimal for Longs and downright dangerous for Shorts.

We've been refactoring the optimizer to decouple the search into Independent Directional Centroids:

The IS parameter search grid scans and computes parameter plateaus for Longs and Shorts independently (different RSI cutoffs, different band stretch multipliers per side).

The OOS Walk-Forward test validates each side on its own merit.

If only one side demonstrates statistically valid alpha in OOS (e.g. Longs pass all WFO hurdles but Shorts fail), the candidate gets tagged as BUY\_ONLY rather than forcing both sides or killing the entire setup.

For those of you running systematic books:

Do you optimize long and short rule parameters independently as standard practice, or do you enforce symmetric rules to protect against degree-of-freedom bloat / curve fitting?

If you do decouple them, how do you guard against the optimizer just fitting to the prevailing macro regime (e.g. a 6-month bull market where everything Long looks amazing and everything Short looks bad)?

Do you penalize or prune unidirectional setups (e.g. BUY\_ONLY) in high-correlation baskets to avoid concentrated directional exposure?

Would love to hear how other teams handle this balance between directional specialization and overfitting.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Splitting the sides makes sense when the trade data shows that big a gap, but it doubles your settings, so I'd count that in how many versions you've tried. The risk I'd worry about most is that a BUY\_ONLY result in a rising market may just be exposure to the basket, so I'd compare it with simply holding the same coins. I'd also require the split to show up in a falling or choppy stretch before trusting it, and keep a period aside that you never tuned on. Cymetica's Backtest Labs has a fee setting and a held out stretch of data for checks like that.

replies.author: Trader_for_earner
replies.body:
Completely agree on the degrees of freedom penalty — splitting by side essentially doubles the parameter space, so treating it like an unpenalized optimization is an easy path to overfitting.

That's actually why I run rolling Walk-Forward Optimization (WFO) with locked out-of-sample stretches rather than just relying on in-sample splits. Interestingly, the directional bias often goes the opposite way in our data: a lot of the surviving setups ended up strictly SELL\_ONLY (fading blow-offs/extensions) because long mean-reversion got chopped to death even in neutral regimes.

Comparing against a naive buy-and-hold benchmark and testing across distinct market regimes (especially chop vs. sustained trends) is a great reminder. Appreciate the thoughtful feedback!

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Interesting that it flipped to SELL\_ONLY. The same caution applies in reverse: if the test period was mostly falling, short setups can look good just from being short the basket. I'd check that the SELL\_ONLY ones also hold up in a rising stretch before trusting them.

replies.author: Trader_for_earner
replies.body:
100% agreed — passive short beta in a down market is a classic trap.

We address that by conditioning evaluation on isolated regime states rather than whole calendar stretches: mean-reversion shorts are filtered out during strong bull trends, and they only qualify if their win rate and expectancy hold up when fading local exhaustion in neutral/mixed chop.

Plus, in live execution we enforce strict directional short caps so the portfolio never ends up carrying unhedged macro short beta into a squeeze.

Running a formal benchmark-beta adjustment against rising BTC/ETH regimes is definitely a smart addition to the validation checklist. Cheers!
